# Conventions every tool shares {#sec-conventions}

The FUSION2 tools share one option parser, one point filter, and one set
of rules for units, missing values, coordinate systems, and table output.
This chapter covers those shared rules once, so the tool chapters can
focus on what each tool does.

## Command-line syntax

Every tool takes its main input as a **positional** argument, placed on
the command line with no option name in front of it. Everything else is an
option (`/name:value`) or a flag (`/name`):

```bat
clipdata my_tile.laz /output:out/box.las /extent:1023780,598900,1023880,599000
```

Three spellings are accepted for every option and flag, and they can be
mixed on one command line:

| Style | Option | Flag |
|:--------------|:----------|:----------|
| Windows (used in this manual) | `/cellsize:2` | `/first` |
| Single dash | `-cellsize 2` | `-first` |
| Double dash | `--cellsize=2` | `--first` |

: The three accepted option spellings. {#tbl-option-styles}

Option names are not case-sensitive. A tool run with `/?`, `-h`, or
`--help` prints its options and exits; @sec-tool-help lists that help for
every tool. A misspelled option name is not reported as an error; the
tool ignores it and uses the option's default, so check a new command's
console output for the settings it actually used.

In the Windows Command Prompt, a long command can continue onto the next
line with `^` at the end of a line. The worked examples use this layout,
one option per line. In PowerShell, use a backtick (`` ` ``) instead, or
put the whole command on one line.

## Inputs: one file or a whole folder

Every tool that reads points accepts either a single `.las`/`.laz` file or
a folder. Given a folder, the tool reads every LAS/LAZ file in it as one
combined point cloud. LAS versions 1.0 through 1.4 are read, compressed
(LAZ) or not. A COPC file (a LAZ file with a built-in spatial index) is
read like any other LAZ file; `gridmetrics`' batch mode also uses its
index to read only the parts each tile needs (@sec-many-tiles).
`gridmetrics` also accepts a single surface raster in place of points,
counting each pixel as one return (@sec-gridmetrics-surface).

Tools that need a ground surface (`/ground:`) accept a single raster
(GeoTIFF, ERDAS Imagine, or ENVI) or a folder of raster tiles. A folder is
joined on the fly into one virtual raster, so a tiled DEM delivery can be
used as is.

## Outputs

Create output folders before running a tool. `gridmetrics` creates a
missing `/outdir` folder, but other tools do not, and some of them exit
without an error message and without writing their output when the
folder is missing.

Rasters are written as GeoTIFF, with each band named (for example
`elev_p95` or `canopy_cover`) so GIS software and R show the band names.
Point clouds are written as LAS or LAZ, chosen by the output file's
extension. They keep the input's point format, scale, offsets, GPS-time
type, and coordinate system.

Every raster-producing tool (`gridmetrics`, `densitymetrics`,
`canopymodel`, `groundfilter`, `returndensity`, `topometrics`,
`gridsurfacestats`) can also write its cell values as a table:

- `/output-table:<path>` writes one row per cell. The file extension
  picks the format: `.csv` for a comma-separated file, `.sqlite` for a
  SQLite database table.
- `/noraster` skips the GeoTIFF and writes only the table. It is only
  valid together with `/output-table`, since a run must produce at least
  one output.

## Point filtering: `/class` and `/return` {#sec-point-filtering}

Every tool that reads points (`gridmetrics`, `cloudmetrics`,
`canopymodel`, `groundfilter`, `clipdata`, `filterdata`, `thindata`,
`returndensity`, `densitymetrics`, and point-reading stages run by
`pipeline`) filters them the same way before doing anything else.

`/class:<spec>` chooses which ASPRS point classes to keep:

| Setting | Points kept |
|:-----------------|:------------------------|
| omitted (default) | every class except the noise classes 7 (low point) and 18 (high noise) |
| `/class:all` or `/class:*` | every class, including 7 and 18 |
| `/class:2,3,4,5` or `/class:1-5` | only the listed classes (lists, ranges, or both) |
| `/class:~7,9,18` | every class except the listed ones (replaces the default 7 and 18) |

: `/class` settings. {#tbl-class-filter}

`/return:<spec>` chooses which returns of each laser pulse to keep:

| Setting | Returns kept |
|:-----------------|:------------------------|
| omitted (default) | every return |
| `/return:1` or `/return:1,2` or `/return:1-2` | the listed return numbers |
| `/return:first` | the first return of each pulse |
| `/return:last` | the last return of each pulse |
| `/return:only` | returns of pulses that produced a single return |
| `/return:intermediate` | returns that are neither first nor last |

: `/return` settings. {#tbl-return-filter}

Points flagged as withheld in the LAS file are always dropped, whatever
`/class` says.

## Units

The tools do no unit conversion. Every distance, height, and cell size is
in the input's own units: feet for a point cloud in a feet-based
projection, meters for one in a meter-based projection. The example tile
in this manual is in US survey feet, so `/cellsize:10` means 10 ft cells
and `/minht:2` means 2 ft above ground. On a meter-based tile the same
commands would mean 10 m cells and 2 m.

Density outputs are points per square unit of the input: points per
square foot for the example tile.

## Heights above ground

Tools that report heights (`gridmetrics`, `cloudmetrics`, `canopymodel`,
`densitymetrics`, `clipdata` with `/minz`/`/maxz`) subtract the ground
elevation beneath each point, read from the `/ground` raster by bilinear
interpolation between the four nearest cell centers. A point up to one
cell outside the ground raster uses the raster's edge value. A point
further outside gets no height and is left out.

`/minht` sets the height below which points are left out of the height
statistics (default 2). `/heightcut` sets the height that separates
canopy from non-canopy returns for canopy cover (it defaults to `/minht`).

## Missing values: `/nodata` and `/noheight`

`gridmetrics` and `cloudmetrics` distinguish two kinds of empty:

- **No points at all** (`/nodata`, default `NA`): nothing landed in the
  cell or plot. Every value is written as `NA`, including point counts.
- **Points, but none above `/minht`** (`/noheight`, default `0`): the
  height and intensity statistics are written as `0`, which is a real
  answer ("no canopy here"). Canopy cover and point counts are computed
  normally.

Both options take `NA` or a number such as `0` or `-9999`. In GeoTIFF
output, `NA` is stored as NaN and registered as the file's NoData value,
so R (`terra`), Python (`rasterio`), and GIS software read those cells as
missing without extra settings. @sec-metrics gives the full rule.

## Coordinate systems

Outputs carry the input's coordinate system. Rasters get it as GeoTIFF
georeferencing. Point clouds keep it in the same form the input used,
either a WKT record or GeoTIFF keys. Rasters derived from other rasters
(`topometrics`, `gridsurfacestats`, `treeseg`) inherit their input
raster's coordinate system. Tables of tree tops and crowns
(`canopymaxima`, `treeseg`) give coordinates in that same system. The
worked examples check that every raster and point cloud output has one.
